title: Make It Look Like What It Does
intro: Affordances show what something **is**. Signifiers show what it **does**. When either is broken, users stop trusting your interface.

learn.title: Affordances vs. signifiers
learn.text:
**Affordance** = the visual form that signals what an element is and how to interact with it. A button that looks raised and clickable has a strong affordance.

**Signifier** = the label, icon, or cue that tells users what will happen. A button labeled "Download Report" has a clear signifier.

The author's test for "intuitive" design: **When someone sees this, do they know what to do?** If not, it's broken.

In an informal study, the author showed a button to 100 people. All 100 said they'd click it. Rule of thumb: if 95 out of 100 people say it "looks like a button," the affordance is strong.

try.q: A raised, rounded element with a slight gradient — that's an example of:
options: Strong affordance
Strong signifier
Good accessibility
Visual hierarchy
try.explain: The visual form signals 'this is clickable' — that's an affordance. The label on it would be the signifier.

learn.title: Weak affordances — when things don't look like what they are
learn.text:
These patterns look clean in Figma but fail with real users:

→ **Single-line inputs with no border** — users don't see them as input fields
→ **Buttons styled as plain text** — users don't know they can click
→ **Floating labels** used as the only hint — users miss the interaction

The core problem: if users must **stop and think about what something is**, the affordance is weak.

Consistency matters across the whole UI. Tabs should look like tabs. Toggles should look like toggles. Input fields should look like places to type.

try.q: A text input with no visible border — why is this a problem?
options: Users don't recognize it as a place to type
It breaks on mobile browsers
Screen readers can't detect it
It violates WCAG color contrast
try.explain: Without visual borders, the affordance is weak — users literally don't see it as an input field.

learn.title: Broken signifiers — when labels lie
learn.text:
A signifier mismatch is when an element's label doesn't match what it actually does:

→ A "Download" button that opens a form first
→ A "Learn More" link that actually means "Subscribe"
→ A text-like element that opens a modal

These mismatches **destroy trust**. Users hesitate, feel tricked, and stop exploring.

The fix is simple: **if it looks like a button and says "Download," it should download.** No extra steps, no surprises.

When a product feels "not intuitive," check two things first:
1. Do elements look like what they are? (affordance)
2. Do labels accurately describe what will happen? (signifier)

try.q: A button says "Download" but first opens a registration form. What's the problem?
options: The signifier is deceptive
The affordance is weak
The button needs a better icon
The form should load faster
try.explain: The label promises one action but delivers another. This is a signifier mismatch — a dark pattern that erodes trust. (The label doesn't match the action.)

test.q: What's the difference between an affordance and a signifier?
options: Affordance = what it looks like (is). Signifier = what it says it does
Affordance = the label. Signifier = the visual design
Affordance = for sighted users. Signifier = for people using screen readers
They're the same thing, just different terminology
test.explain: Affordance is the visual form (looks clickable). Signifier is the label/cue (says what happens when you click).

test.q: What's the author's diagnostic test for intuitive design?
options: "When someone sees this, do they know what to do?"
"Can users complete the task in under 3 seconds?"
"Does it follow Material Design guidelines?"
"Do users rate it 4+ stars in satisfaction surveys?"
test.explain: If users can't tell what to do just by looking, the design has broken affordances or signifiers.

test.q: Which of these is an example of a weak affordance?
options: A button styled as plain text with no visual distinction
A button with a clear label but wrong color
A button that's too small to tap on mobile
A button with an icon but no label
test.explain: A button that looks like plain text doesn't signal 'clickable' — users don't know it's interactive.

test.q: "Learn More" that actually leads to a subscription page is an example of:
options: A deceptive signifier
A weak affordance
Bad information architecture
A missing tooltip
test.explain: The label promises information but delivers a sales page. That's a broken signifier that erodes user trust. (The label lies about what happens.)

test.q: When a product feels "not intuitive," what should you check first?
options: Do elements look like what they are, and do labels match what happens?
Is the visual design consistent with the brand guidelines and the design system?
Are all interactions animated smoothly?
Does it follow the latest design trends?
test.explain: Check affordances (do things look like what they are?) and signifiers (do labels match actions?). These are the two most common causes of confusion.
